ctr.credit: Xia X, Zhu X, Zhu Y, et al. Front Surg. 2024;10:1229522 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 2
ctr.caption: Laryngotracheal release, then the completed larynx-to-trachea anastomosis, after an en bloc resection that took the anterolateral cricoid with the upper tracheal rings. Note how little tension the suture line is under once both ends are released (panel C). This is a malignant extended resection, not a benign Type B CTR.

tracheal-resection.credit: Xia X, Zhu X, Zhu Y, et al. Front Surg. 2024;10:1229522 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 2
tracheal-resection.caption: Sequence from a long-segment (more than six rings) tracheal sleeve resection: release of the trachea and larynx (A), the end-to-end anastomosis done with running 2-0 polypropylene (B), and the tension-free result (C). The authors used a running suture; many surgeons prefer interrupted sutures. Panel D is the 6-month endoscopic check.

central-neck.credit: Shi Q, Xu J, Fang J, et al. Front Endocrinol. 2022;13:918741 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 2
central-neck.caption: Right paratracheal (level VI) dissection, panel by panel. The right RLN is dissected free and kept lateral, toward the common carotid, while the level VIa and VIb nodal tissue behind it is cleared. Colored lines mark the dissection borders and arrows mark the vagus (V1) and RLN (R1, R2) stimulation points.

central-neck.credit: Shi Q, Xu J, Fang J, et al. Front Endocrinol. 2022;13:918741 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 3
central-neck.caption: The right central compartment after the paratracheal packet is removed. The RLN, its lateral branches, and the thin vascular fascia between the nerve and the carotid are still intact. This is what a clean, nerve-sparing level VI bed should look like.

central-neck.credit: Shi Q, Xu J, Fang J, et al. Front Endocrinol. 2022;13:918741 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 4
central-neck.caption: Saving the right inferior parathyroid during central neck dissection. The gland and its vascular pedicle are identified once the lobe is lifted. The gland stays on the thyrothymic (sternothyroid) ligament, which is fanned out away from the specimen. Arrows label the thyroid lobe, the parathyroid, its blood supply, and the RLN.

facial-nerve-reanimation.credit: Jeong J, Almansoori AA, Park HS, et al. Maxillofac Plast Reconstr Surg. 2018;40(1):22 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 3
facial-nerve-reanimation.caption: Harvesting and routing a cross-face sural nerve graft. A submucosal tunnel is made through the upper vestibule, a sural nerve about 20 cm long is harvested, and the graft is passed through the tunnel. Note how much length a cross-face graft needs.

facial-nerve-reanimation.credit: Jeong J, Almansoori AA, Park HS, et al. Maxillofac Plast Reconstr Surg. 2018;40(1):22 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 4
facial-nerve-reanimation.caption: Microscope views of the coaptation. The graft is lined up with the buccal branch, the recipient branch is prepared, and the repair is closed with a few fine epineurial sutures. Notice how few sutures are used and how little the nerve ends are handled.

otoplasty.caption: A posterior-approach otoplasty, step by step: the protruding ear before surgery, the postauricular skin incision with the fascioperichondrial layer raised, the plane prepared for the antihelical sutures, and the flap turned over the suture line before closure. The flap covers the permanent sutures to lower the risk of extrusion.

frontal-sinus-trauma.credit: Kim I, Kim JM, Kim J, et al. Maxillofac Plast Reconstr Surg. 2024;46(1):4 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 3
frontal-sinus-trauma.caption: Obliteration sequence for a combined anterior- and posterior-table fracture: the anterior table is osteotomized and lifted, the sinus is stripped of mucosa, and the cavity is filled (here with hydroxyapatite cement) before the anterior wall is replaced. Notice that obliteration depends on complete mucosal removal from every recess.

frontal-sinus-trauma.credit: Kim I, Kim JM, Kim J, et al. Maxillofac Plast Reconstr Surg. 2024;46(1):4 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 4
frontal-sinus-trauma.caption: Cranialization: with the anterior table elevated, the posterior table has been removed so the frontal dura is exposed and the brain can expand forward into the old sinus space; the anterior table is then put back. Look at the exposed dura, which you inspect for tears before closing.

styloidectomy.credit: Matsumoto F, Kase K, Kasai M, et al. Head Face Med. 2012;8:21 (CC BY 2.0) — Fig. 2
styloidectomy.caption: Endoscope-assisted transoral view through the tonsillar fossa: the elongated styloid process has been dissected free of its soft-tissue cuff and is ready to be removed (arrow). Notice how the endoscope magnifies the deep fossa, which helps you stay on bone.

neck-dissection.credit: Abakay MA, Güneş S, Küçük C, et al. Turk Arch Otorhinolaryngol. 2020;58(3):149-154 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 1
neck-dissection.caption: Fresh-cadaver right neck after subplatysmal flaps are raised, with the main surface landmarks marked. This is a cadaver dissection, not a live case; use it to set the boundaries of the field before you strip the fascia off the SCM.

neck-dissection.credit: Abakay MA, Güneş S, Küçük C, et al. Turk Arch Otorhinolaryngol. 2020;58(3):149-154 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 4
neck-dissection.caption: Fresh-cadaver right neck with the SCM detached and retracted, showing the accessory nerve branching in the anterior triangle and its relationship to nearby structures. Notice how the nerve's course can vary in the upper neck, so find it before you clear level II.

tors.credit: Granell J, Mendez-Benegassi I, Millas T, et al. Case Rep Otolaryngol. 2014;2014:497528 (CC BY) — Fig. 1
tors.caption: Robotic views of a radical tonsillectomy, with spatula cautery in the right arm and a Maryland dissector in the left: the tumor, the soft-palate incision, the lateral dissection into the parapharyngeal plane, and the medial, superior and inferior resection limits. Notice how the lateral plane is developed outside the constrictor.

tors.credit: Granell J, Mendez-Benegassi I, Millas T, et al. Case Rep Otolaryngol. 2014;2014:497528 (CC BY) — Fig. 2
tors.caption: Diagram of the full cut sequence for a TORS radical tonsillectomy, from the first mucosal incision to the last deep medial cut. Use it as a roadmap to keep the order of the cuts straight.

total-laryngectomy.credit: Grošelj A, Tancer I, Jerman A, et al. Front Oncol. 2024;13:1284266 (CC BY) — Fig. 3
total-laryngectomy.caption: Four-panel sequence of the pharyngeal defect after total laryngectomy with partial pharyngectomy: the preserved epiglottis (asterisk) is mobilized and slid down to close the gap and form the neopharynx. This is a sliding-epiglottis variant of closure, so use it to see the defect and the tension-free closure principle rather than standard primary closure.

free-flap-basics.credit: Tomasetti PE, Kuttenberger J, Meroni M, et al. Plast Aesthet Res. 2021;8:12 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 1
free-flap-basics.caption: Radial forearm flap from skin markings through harvest, then split into two skin paddles that each keep their own perforators. Notice the pedicle running with the radial artery and how each paddle stays tied to a perforator.

free-flap-basics.credit: Tomasetti PE, Kuttenberger J, Meroni M, et al. Plast Aesthet Res. 2021;8:12 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 3
free-flap-basics.caption: Medial sural artery perforator (calf) flap: skin markings, the perforator isolated during dissection, and the harvested flap. Follow the perforator back toward its source vessel to see how pedicle length is gained.

free-flap-basics.credit: Tomasetti PE, Kuttenberger J, Meroni M, et al. Plast Aesthet Res. 2021;8:12 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 9
free-flap-basics.caption: Fibula free flap with two perforator-based skin paddles: markings, harvest, and several osteotomies that shape the bone to fit the mandibular defect. Notice how the skin paddles stay attached to the bone segments through their perforators.

zenker.credit: Arens C, Herrmann IF, Rohrbach S, et al. GMS Curr Top Otorhinolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2015;14:Doc02 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 12
zenker.caption: Three panels of a Zenker diverticulum: the pouch opening on flexible endoscopy, then the same anatomy through a seated diverticuloscope, then a small residual pouch 6 months after endoscopic stapling. In the middle panel, see how the scope's two blades split the esophageal lumen from the pouch so the common wall (the bar) sits between them.

vestibular-schwannoma.credit: Bi Y, Ni Y, Gao D, et al. Front Oncol. 2022;11:774462 (CC BY) — Fig. 4
vestibular-schwannoma.caption: A retrosigmoid case with a right vestibular schwannoma extending into the internal auditory canal and a high-riding jugular bulb. Preoperative MRI and CT are followed by drilling of the posterior canal wall, a remnant at the fundus that the microscope cannot see but an angled endoscope can, and finally VII and VIII left intact after the fundal tumor is removed.

stapedotomy.credit: Abdullah NE, Nafie TA, Mohammed AF, et al. Egypt J Otolaryngol. 2021;37:81 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 2
stapedotomy.caption: Transcanal endoscopic view after the stapes crura have been fractured and removed, leaving the footplate in the oval window (O) exposed. Note the clear view of the footplate before any fenestra is made.

stapedotomy.credit: Abdullah NE, Nafie TA, Mohammed AF, et al. Egypt J Otolaryngol. 2021;37:81 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 3
stapedotomy.caption: Endoscopic view of the fenestra being made in the center of the footplate (black circle). Notice the small, central opening that leaves the footplate rim intact.

stapedotomy.credit: Abdullah NE, Nafie TA, Mohammed AF, et al. Egypt J Otolaryngol. 2021;37:81 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 4
stapedotomy.caption: Teflon piston in place: its loop hooks over the long process of the incus and the shaft drops into the fenestra. Check that the shaft sits centerd in the opening, not resting on the footplate edge.

tegmen-repair.credit: Thomeer HGXM, Schreurs C, van Doormaal TPC, et al. Front Surg. 2020;7:21 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 1
tegmen-repair.caption: Middle fossa repair of a right tegmen tympani meningocele shown in stages: the bony defect, bone wax in the defect, bone dust over the tegmen with a dural patch, and fascia placed between the layers. A good example of layered closure from above.

tegmen-repair.credit: Thomeer HGXM, Schreurs C, van Doormaal TPC, et al. Front Surg. 2020;7:21 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 2
tegmen-repair.caption: Transmastoid repair of a left tegmen mastoideum defect: the defect is exposed, the dura is patched, a bone chip rebuilds the tegmen, and the cavity is filled with bone dust behind a rebuilt canal wall. Notice that this corridor only reaches defects over the mastoid.

tympanoplasty.credit: Takahashi M, Motegi M, Yamamoto K, et al. J Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2022;51:45 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 1
tympanoplasty.caption: Six-panel 0° endoscopic sequence of an interlay type I tympanoplasty: canal incision, finding the annulus, lifting the epithelial layer off the drum and around the perforation, and placing the graft between the epithelial and fibrous layers. Use it to follow how the plane next to the annulus is found and raised.

tympanoplasty.credit: Takahashi M, Motegi M, Yamamoto K, et al. J Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2022;51:45 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 2
tympanoplasty.caption: Endoscopic views of an ear with an overhanging anteroinferior canal wall, before and after the bulge is drilled down, and the healed drum one year later. Shows why canalplasty is done when the anterior edge of the perforation cannot be seen.

middle-fossa-skull-base.credit: Tayebi Meybodi A, Mignucci-Jiménez G, Lawton MT, et al. Front Surg. 2023;10:1132784 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 1
middle-fossa-skull-base.caption: Cadaver dissection of the right middle fossa floor with the temporal dura lifted, shown before and after drilling, with the triangles and the nerves and vessels on the floor labelled. Use it to learn where the floor landmarks lie relative to each other before placing the retractor.

retrosigmoid-skull-base.credit: Jia C, Xu C, Wang M, et al. Front Surg. 2022;9:889402 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 3
retrosigmoid-skull-base.caption: Lateral-type vestibular schwannoma: fused MRI/CT planning with a 'lateral safe line', the navigation-predicted drilling limit, intraoperative views of the tumor at the fundus, and postoperative imaging showing an intact labyrinth. Shows how far the posterior IAC wall can be drilled without opening the inner ear.

retrosigmoid-skull-base.credit: Jia C, Xu C, Wang M, et al. Front Surg. 2022;9:889402 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 2
retrosigmoid-skull-base.caption: Medial-type case: planning images and navigation, then endoscopic views of drilling deep canal bone and removing leftover tumor at the fundus, with postoperative MRI/CT. Notice how an angled endoscope shows the fundus that the microscope cannot see.

supraglottoplasty.credit: Cialente F, Meucci D, Tropiano ML, et al. Children (Basel). 2021;8(12):1120 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 1
supraglottoplasty.caption: Endoscopic view of severe laryngomalacia. Look for the short aryepiglottic folds and the redundant arytenoid mucosa that collapse into the airway; these are what the operation divides and trims.

laryngotracheal-cleft-repair.credit: Tang X, Yang Y, Zhang Z, et al. Front Pediatr. 2023;11:1113894 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 2
laryngotracheal-cleft-repair.caption: Endoscopic view of a fresh incision along the mucosal edge of an interarytenoid cleft. The edges are freshened to raw tissue so that they will heal together once closed.

laryngotracheal-cleft-repair.credit: Tang X, Yang Y, Zhang Z, et al. Front Pediatr. 2023;11:1113894 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 3
laryngotracheal-cleft-repair.caption: Nine-panel endoscopic sequence of a percutaneous needle-and-suture repair of a type 1 cleft: sutures pass through each cleft edge and are tied on the airway side. Follow how the edges are brought together to give a smooth posterior glottic surface.

tonsillectomy-adenoidectomy.credit: Omer GL, Abdullah AS, Ali SS, et al. Children (Basel). 2025;12(10):1393 (CC BY) — Fig. 1
tonsillectomy-adenoidectomy.caption: Intraoperative transnasal endoscopic views after a conventional adenoidectomy: residual adenoid still blocks the right choana, is cleared with a microdebrider, bleeding is controlled with coblation, and the nasopharynx ends up clear. Residual tissue near the choana is easy to miss without the endoscope.

adenoidectomy.credit: Omer GL, Abdullah AS, Ali SS, et al. Children (Basel). 2025;12(10):1393 (CC BY) — Fig. 1
adenoidectomy.caption: Intraoperative transnasal endoscopic views after a conventional adenoidectomy: residual adenoid still blocks the right choana, is cleared with a microdebrider, bleeding is controlled with coblation, and the nasopharynx ends up clear. Residual tissue near the choana is easy to miss without the endoscope.

branchial.credit: Reddy A, Valika T, Maddalozzo J. J Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2020;49:55 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 1
branchial.caption: Schematic of a second branchial cleft fistula course: the tract climbs between the internal and external carotid arteries and enters the oropharynx just above and lateral to the greater cornu of the hyoid. That course is why the tract is followed superiorly between the carotids toward the tonsillar fossa.

branchial.credit: Han Y, Yang RQ, Hong L, et al. BMC Surg. 2021;21:306 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 4
branchial.caption: Intraoperative views of a first branchial cleft fistula excision: the facial nerve is identified with the larger tract running deep to it, a blind pouch tracks along the masseter, and the roughly 6 cm specimen contains cartilage. Notice that the nerve is found first, before the tract is followed.

draf.credit: Zhao Y, Liu J, Yang D, et al. Front Surg. 2022;9:871635 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 2
draf.caption: Cadaver step sequence for an endoscopic modified Lothrop (Draf III): a roughly 2 × 2 cm superior septal window, exposure of the bone above both middle-turbinate axillae, drilling along that path, and the final common frontal opening. Note that the olfactory filaments and the frontal recesses stay unexposed.

draf.credit: Zhao Y, Liu J, Yang D, et al. Front Surg. 2022;9:871635 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 3
draf.caption: Patient Draf III sequence: after the septal window, bone is drilled anteriorly to open both frontal sinus floors and reach a frontal tumor, ending with a wide common neo-ostium. Compare it with the cadaver steps to see the same landmarks in live tissue.

endoscopic-pituitary.credit: Baussart B, Venier A, Jouinot A, et al. Front Oncol. 2022;12:1067312 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 1
endoscopic-pituitary.caption: Endoscopic sequence from the sphenoid stage (labeled sella, tuberculum, clivus, cavernous sinus) to the opened sellar floor and the bed after tumor removal. Note that the bony opening is wider than the rectangular dural opening, which leaves an epidural rim for the later closure.

endoscopic-pituitary.credit: Baussart B, Venier A, Jouinot A, et al. Front Oncol. 2022;12:1067312 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 5
endoscopic-pituitary.caption: Multilayer closure in a high-risk case: intrasellar muscle, then fascia lata wedged epidurally with a bone graft, then a pedicled nasoseptal flap held by a Foley balloon, with a postoperative MRI. Notice how each layer rests on bare bone or in the epidural space.

endoscopic-sinus-surgery.credit: Araujo Filho BC, Pinheiro-Neto CD, Ramos HF, et al. Braz J Otorhinolaryngol. 2011;77(1):33-38 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 5
endoscopic-sinus-surgery.caption: Cadaver endoscopic view, with the lamina papyracea removed, of the right anterior ethmoidal artery in its bony canal as it passes from the orbit toward the skull base. Note how close it is to the ethmoid roof, which is why you skeletonize here rather than strip.

inferior-turbinate-reduction.credit: Neri G, Cazzato F, Vestrini E, et al. Turbinate Surgery in Chronic Rhinosinusitis. In: Gendeh BS, Turkalj M, eds. Rhinosinusitis. IntechOpen; 2019 (CC BY 3.0) — Fig. 7
inferior-turbinate-reduction.caption: Cold inferior turbinoplasty (Mabry technique): incision at the anterior turbinate, elevation of a medial mucosal flap, removal of the inferior and lateral bone and soft tissue, then the medial mucosa rolled into a 'neoturbinate'. Note that the medial mucosa is kept.

inferior-turbinate-reduction.credit: Neri G, Cazzato F, Vestrini E, et al. Turbinate Surgery in Chronic Rhinosinusitis. In: Gendeh BS, Turkalj M, eds. Rhinosinusitis. IntechOpen; 2019 (CC BY 3.0) — Fig. 5
inferior-turbinate-reduction.caption: Drawing of a lateral outfracture of the inferior turbinate, pushing the turbinate toward the lateral nasal wall to widen the inferior airway. It is often combined with a volume-reduction technique.

inferior-turbinate-reduction.credit: Neri G, Cazzato F, Vestrini E, et al. Turbinate Surgery in Chronic Rhinosinusitis. In: Gendeh BS, Turkalj M, eds. Rhinosinusitis. IntechOpen; 2019 (CC BY 3.0) — Fig. 4
inferior-turbinate-reduction.caption: Drawing of a partial inferior turbinectomy, showing how much of the turbinate is removed. Compare it with the total turbinectomy in the same chapter to see why only a limited resection is advised.

maxillary-antrostomy.credit: Phatak S, Agrawal R. Rhinosinusitis: How Common Are Anatomical Variations Responsible? In: Gendeh BS, Turkalj M, eds. Rhinosinusitis. IntechOpen; 2019 (CC BY 3.0) — Fig. 15
maxillary-antrostomy.caption: Endoscopic view of two accessory maxillary ostia in the posterior fontanelle. They are what an antrostomy must join to the natural ostium so that mucus does not recirculate between the two openings.

orbital-abscess.credit: Ramli FS, Jumaat AF, Zahedi FD. Sinusitis. 2025;9(2):21 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 4
orbital-abscess.caption: Intraoperative endoscopic views from a child's case: pus draining from the opened maxillary sinus, then from the subperiosteal orbital space once the lamina is opened. Both the sinus source and the orbital collection are drained in the same sitting.

spa-ligation.credit: Liu X, Wang P, Li M, et al. Front Surg. 2023;10:1203409 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 1
spa-ligation.caption: A cadaver view of the posterior nasal septal artery, a branch of the sphenopalatine artery, crossing the face of the sphenoid, then a live case where it bleeds and is controlled with bipolar forceps. This shows why the septal branch must be found and treated, not just the lateral trunk.

spa-ligation.credit: Araujo Filho BC, Pinheiro-Neto CD, Ramos HF, et al. Braz J Otorhinolaryngol. 2011;77(1):33-38 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 4
spa-ligation.caption: Cadaver endoscopic view of a clip on the left anterior ethmoidal artery in the subperiosteal orbital plane. This is the rescue option when bleeding comes from a superior or anterior ethmoidal source rather than the sphenopalatine system.

septoplasty.credit: Lin YT. Septoplasty: Endoscopic and Open Techniques. In: Heinbockel T, Gendeh BS, eds. Sino-Nasal and Olfactory System Disorders. IntechOpen; 2020 (CC BY 3.0) — Fig. 2
septoplasty.caption: Diagram of the Killian and hemitransfixion incisions for raising mucoperichondrial flaps, a septotomy that keeps an adequate L-strut, and a cut at the bony-cartilaginous junction. The thing to notice is how much dorsal and caudal cartilage must stay.

septoplasty.credit: Lin YT. Septoplasty: Endoscopic and Open Techniques. In: Heinbockel T, Gendeh BS, eds. Sino-Nasal and Olfactory System Disorders. IntechOpen; 2020 (CC BY 3.0) — Fig. 3
septoplasty.caption: Correcting a caudal cartilage curve in three steps: a partial-thickness score on the concave side, repositioning to the midline to see the overlap, then trimming the excess. This is how the caudal septum is brought to a stable midline without weakening support.

csf-nasoseptal.credit: Baussart B, Venier A, Jouinot A, et al. Front Oncol. 2022;12:1067312 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 5
csf-nasoseptal.caption: Endoscopic multilayer sellar repair: a fascia lata graft placed epidurally and locked with bone, covered by a rotated nasoseptal flap and supported by a Foley balloon. This is the inlay-then-onlay-then-vascularized-flap order, with a balloon for support.

completion-thyroidectomy.credit: Pais Moreira H, Viegas V, Louro H, et al. Cureus. 2025;17(8):e89908 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 2
completion-thyroidectomy.caption: A non-recurrent laryngeal nerve (arrow) running straight from the vagus to the cricothyroid junction in a patient with an aberrant right subclavian artery. On the right side, check the CT for this vascular anomaly and do not divide transverse bands at the level of the inferior thyroid artery until the nerve is found.

completion-thyroidectomy.credit: Huang J, He Y, Wang Y, et al. Front Endocrinol (Lausanne). 2023;14:1086367 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 4
completion-thyroidectomy.caption: White-light and autofluorescence views of a superior parathyroid kept in place after a superior thyroid artery branch is divided, and of inferior glands after the inferior vessels are taken. In a completion case these may be the only glands left, so keep them on their blood supply.

four-gland.credit: Huang J, He Y, Wang Y, et al. Front Endocrinol (Lausanne). 2023;14:1086367 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 3
four-gland.caption: Dorsal thyroid surface and the thyrothymic ligament under white light and near-infrared autofluorescence, showing a gland lying low and a gland within the thymus. Follow the thyrothymic ligament down to find a low or intrathymic inferior gland.

four-gland.credit: Huang J, He Y, Wang Y, et al. Front Endocrinol (Lausanne). 2023;14:1086367 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 1
four-gland.caption: Schematic sorting parathyroid glands by where they turn up during the operation, from the usual sites to ectopic and intrathymic ones. Use it as a checklist of where to look when a gland is missing.

parathyroidectomy.credit: Huang J, He Y, Wang Y, et al. Front Endocrinol (Lausanne). 2023;14:1086367 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 2
parathyroidectomy.caption: Angles for imaging the right superior and inferior glands, with matched white-light and autofluorescence frames. A true parathyroid lights up brightly compared with fat, nodes or thyroid tissue, which helps with the 'is this a gland?' question.

parotidectomy.credit: Lee GM, Fong PY, Tan LTH, et al. Arch Otorhinolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2023;7(1):5 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 1
parotidectomy.caption: Four panels from a parotid case with unusual nerve anatomy: CT showing the tumor beside the retromandibular vein, the main trunk curving back toward the tragus, branches draped across the tumor surface, and the intact nerve after excision. It shows why branches are dissected off the tumor capsule under direct vision rather than assumed to run deep to it.

reop-thyroid.credit: Huang J, He Y, Wang Y, et al. Front Endocrinol (Lausanne). 2023;14:1086367 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 5
reop-thyroid.caption: Deep thyroid bed and tracheoesophageal groove explored during central neck dissection, with parathyroids in this area identified by autofluorescence. In scarred re-operations, find and save gland tissue in the groove before you clear the compartment.

sialendoscopy.credit: Filipov I, Cristache CM, Chirila L, et al. J Clin Med. 2025;14(11):3938 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 4
sialendoscopy.caption: Dormia basket holding a salivary stone, then the stone secured within the basket after removal. Open the basket beyond the stone and close it gently, and never pull hard on a stone that is wedged against a narrow duct.

sialendoscopy.credit: Filipov I, Cristache CM, Chirila L, et al. J Clin Med. 2025;14(11):3938 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 2
sialendoscopy.caption: A 9 mm Wharton duct stone: CBCT localization, transoral view while opening the duct onto the stone, and the duct after removal. Stones this large are usually too big to basket and need a transoral duct incision.

sialendoscopy.credit: Filipov I, Cristache CM, Chirila L, et al. J Clin Med. 2025;14(11):3938 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 5
sialendoscopy.caption: Balloon dilation of a Stensen duct stricture with progressive expansion, then a stent left in the duct. Stenting after dilation or ductotomy helps keep the duct open while it heals.

thyroid-lobectomy.credit: Kihara M, Miyauchi A, Fujishima M, et al. Thyroid Res. 2023;16:30 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 2
thyroid-lobectomy.caption: Intraoperative sequence of a right lobectomy in which the recurrent laryngeal nerve runs across the FRONT of the tumor, seen as soon as the sternothyroid is divided and traced to its laryngeal entry at the cricothyroid joint. The lesson: confirm the nerve before dividing any tissue on the lobe surface, because large tumors can displace it anteriorly.

thyroid-lobectomy.credit: Huang J, He Y, Wang Y, et al. Front Endocrinol (Lausanne). 2023;14:1086367 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 6
thyroid-lobectomy.caption: Resected thyroid and central neck specimens checked under autofluorescence for a parathyroid removed by accident. Look over every specimen before it leaves the field, and autotransplant any gland you recover.

total-thyroidectomy.credit: Huang J, He Y, Wang Y, et al. Front Endocrinol (Lausanne). 2023;14:1086367 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 2
total-thyroidectomy.caption: Matched white-light and autofluorescence images of right superior and inferior parathyroids during thyroidectomy. Find and save each gland on its vessels before the lobe is mobilized medially.

total-thyroidectomy.credit: Pais Moreira H, Viegas V, Louro H, et al. Cureus. 2025;17(8):e89908 (CC BY 4.0) — Fig. 2
total-thyroidectomy.caption: Right-sided non-recurrent laryngeal nerve (arrow) leaving the vagus and running directly medially to the cricothyroid junction, found in a patient with an aberrant right subclavian artery. A transverse 'nerve' crossing at the level of the inferior thyroid artery should be presumed to be the laryngeal nerve until proven otherwise.
